subtopics.title: Ionic bonding: transfer, lattice and properties

slots.X: Which electron-transfer events produce the observed ion charges?
slots.Y: Shell arrangement and valency of two elements
slots.Z: Connect charges, electrostatic attraction and resulting formula
slots.W: Learner constructs the causal bridge from electron transfer to stable charge balance

qrt_instances.student_task: Explain why the simple Mg and Cl bonding model leads to MgCl2, without merely citing criss-cross valency.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: Magnesium loses one electron because chlorine needs one
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Calculate ion charge by electron conservation and satisfy overall electroneutrality
qrt_instances.visual_job: Shell diagrams for Mg and Cl with electron counts, but no completed ionic formula
qrt_instances.independent_check: Count donated/accepted electrons and verify net charge is zero

slots.X: What kind of model explains high melting point and conduction in a molten but not solid sample?
slots.Y: Mobile charge carrier condition and ionic lattice constraints
slots.W: Learner chooses a model and checks its assumptions against two observations

qrt_instances.student_task: Given measured conductivity and melting properties, decide whether a lattice of ions is a defensible model and identify missing corroboration.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: Electrical conduction alone proves a compound is ionic
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Compare charge carriers, state and melting behavior; reject model from one observation
qrt_instances.visual_job: Solid/molten particle diagrams with anonymous species and no highlighted preferred model
qrt_instances.independent_check: Check both states and an alternate source of mobile charges

slots.X: Can one conductivity observation establish ionic bonding uniquely?
slots.Y: Comparison of solid state, aqueous state, concentration and chemical reaction possibilities
slots.W: Learner identifies a decisive counterexample and limits the inference

qrt_instances.student_task: A sample gives a conducting aqueous solution but nonconducting solid. Evaluate whether that alone proves the original solid was an ionic compound.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: Any aqueous conductor must have been ionic in its original state
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Test whether an initially molecular substance can form ions by reacting with water; request additional evidence
qrt_instances.visual_job: Evidence chart showing observations and unfilled competing hypothesis columns
qrt_instances.independent_check: Produce a chemically plausible counterexample and specify a discriminating experiment
